opus-5.5.text:
Back in 2016 I was still a PhD student, and our lab simply didn't have a robotic arm. But the question that fascinated me was how an agent could understand and carry out a sequence of interactions with objects. Not just grasping once, but doing several steps in a row, where each step changes the state of the world and sets up the next one.

Without hardware, the natural move was to go into simulation and graphics. We built virtual scenes with 3D object models and let a virtual agent, essentially a hand or a simplified body, interact with them. That let us represent the whole chain: approach the object, make contact, manipulate it, then move on to the next action. Because everything was in a synthetic environment, we could generate a lot of data, control the conditions precisely, and visualize every step, which would have been very hard with a physical setup at that time.

Honestly, it was a constraint-driven choice. If I'd had an arm, I might have gone straight to real experiments and gotten stuck on hardware problems. Being forced into simulation made me think more about the structure of interaction itself: what representation of objects and actions lets you reason over multiple steps. Looking back, that experience shaped a lot of my later belief that simulation and synthetic data are a core path for embodied intelligence, not just a stopgap. The tools back then were much cruder, and the physics was nowhere near today's fidelity, but the basic intuition has stayed with me.

r001.rationale: The response describes a virtual agent, “essentially a hand or a simplified body,” interacting in simulation, but does not clearly identify animating a human hand as the substitute demonstration.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, we had no choice but to get creative. At the time, around 2016, the lab didn't have a robotic arm at all, and buying one was completely out of reach for us. But the whole point of the project was to show that we could understand and reproduce multi-step interaction with objects, like opening a drawer, taking something out, and putting it somewhere else. So we needed some embodiment that could actually touch things.

What we ended up doing was essentially turning humans into the "robot." We had people wear motion capture markers and perform these tasks, and we modeled the human hand and arm as if they were the end effector of a system we were controlling. The perception and planning side was all ours, running on the 3D scene we reconstructed, and then a person would execute the plan step by step, following instructions from the system. It sounds a little silly in retrospect, but it let us validate the hard part, which was the scene understanding and the sequencing of actions, without the hardware.

There was also a simulation component. We built a fairly simple physics environment where the same policies could run on a virtual arm, so we could at least show that the plans were executable in principle. Between the simulated arm and the human stand-in, reviewers could see that the pipeline worked end to end.

Looking back, that constraint actually shaped how I think about research. It forced us to separate the question of what the agent should do from the question of how it physically does it. That separation is still useful to me today, even now that we do have arms in the lab.

r001.rationale: The response describes people performing tasks with motion-capture markers and a human hand and arm acting as the system’s end effector, but it does not identify animation of a human hand as the substitute demonstration.
